---
title: "Week 10 — Map Visualization — Module II"
---

> Points, density and distance. Module I colored regions somebody else had already drawn. This module works with raw point locations, where the groups and surfaces on the map are things you compute — and every computation takes a parameter you chose.

## 📖 Background & Motivation

A choropleth starts with regions someone else defined: states, counties, census tracts. Your decisions were which measure to show and how to color it. Point data arrives with none of that structure. A few thousand latitude and longitude pairs are not divided into anything, so if you want neighborhoods, catchments or clusters you have to construct them — and that is a modeling decision rather than a cartographic one.

This module works through what you can ask of points that you cannot ask of polygons. How crowded is it here, and at what resolution did you decide that? How far is the nearest one, measured how? Which points form groups, under which definition of "close"? Each answer depends on a parameter, and the parameter belongs in the caption alongside the answer.

Distance is where geographic data stops behaving like a scatter plot. Latitude and longitude are angles, not lengths, and a degree of longitude shrinks from about 100 km in southern Florida to 54 km in Alaska. Treating them as a flat grid — which is the first thing most code does — produces results that are wrong in a way nothing reports. We measure how wrong on real data.

The week still ends in a Streamlit dashboard, because that is the delivery format for the final project. But the dashboard is how the work is presented, not what the work is.

---

## 🔎 Learning Objectives

- Recognize overplotting and choose between transparency, aggregation and a density surface.
- Build a density surface from points, and state the resolution that produced it.
- Compute distances on the Earth's surface with haversine, and explain why Euclidean distance on degrees is wrong.
- Cluster point data with DBSCAN, choose `eps` and `min_samples` deliberately, and check the result against something you already know.
- Read "noise" as a category rather than a failure.
- Embed the result in a Streamlit dashboard, and manage performance for many-feature maps.

## 📚 Readings & Resources

- [scikit-learn — clustering](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/clustering.html#dbscan) — DBSCAN, its two parameters, and what it does with points it will not group.
- [scikit-learn — BallTree](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/modules/generated/sklearn.neighbors.BallTree.html) — nearest-neighbor queries, including the `haversine` metric.
- [Folium — quickstart](https://python-visualization.github.io/folium/latest/getting_started.html).
- [streamlit-folium](https://github.com/randyzwitch/streamlit-folium) — embedding folium in Streamlit.
- Shneiderman, [*The Eyes Have It*](https://www.cs.umd.edu/~ben/papers/Shneiderman1996eyes.pdf) (1996) — overview first, zoom and filter, details on demand.

**Sample Data Sources for Practice:**

- `superchargers_us.csv` in this week's materials — 2,264 US Tesla Supercharger sites with coordinates, stall counts and opening dates.
- [OpenStreetMap via Overpass](https://overpass-turbo.eu/) — extract points of a chosen type (cafes, clinics, bus stops) for any area.
- [data.gov](https://data.gov/) — federal, state and local open data, including boundary files and point inventories.
- [Social Explorer](https://www.socialexplorer.com/) — census and ACS tables with matching geographies, tract level and up. A subscription product; check whether the GW library covers it before you rely on it.
- [Census TIGER/Line](https://www.census.gov/geographies/mapping-files/time-series/geo/tiger-line-file.html) — the US boundary files themselves, for every unit from block group to state.
- Any point dataset with latitude and longitude: incidents, stations, sightings, listings.

**The thing to actually do.** Open *How states compare* and read the two maps
as a pair. Florida is second in the country by number of sites and third by
number of stalls; Texas is third by sites and second by stalls. The two maps
put the same two states in a different order, from the same table, because a
site with 40 stalls is not one site's worth of charging. Which of the two you
publish is a claim about what you think a reader wants to know.

Then open *What is nearby* and point at a site in Wyoming, then at one in New
Jersey. The median gap to the nearest other site is 8 km nationally, and the
long lines in the interior are what the median hides.

## 💻 Notebook / App Snippets

### Distance on a sphere

```python
import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import BallTree

EARTH_KM = 6371.0088
tree = BallTree(np.radians(df[["lat", "lon"]].values), metric="haversine")

# k=2 because the nearest point to any point is itself
dist, idx = tree.query(np.radians(df[["lat", "lon"]].values), k=2)
df["nearest_km"] = dist[:, 1] * EARTH_KM
```

Two things silently return nonsense: passing degrees instead of radians, and
forgetting that the result is an angle until you multiply by the radius.

### DBSCAN, done correctly

```python
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN

EPS_KM, MIN_SAMPLES = 50, 5
labels = DBSCAN(eps=EPS_KM / EARTH_KM,          # an angle, not a distance
                min_samples=MIN_SAMPLES,
                metric="haversine").fit_predict(np.radians(coords))
```

Doing it on raw degrees with `eps=50/111` also runs, and is wrong by more the
further north you go. Label `-1` means noise: not an error, a category.

### Comparing two clusterings

```python
from sklearn.metrics import adjusted_rand_score

# Cluster NUMBERS are arbitrary -- DBSCAN hands them out in discovery order --
# so compare the groupings, not the labels.
print(adjusted_rand_score(labels_a, labels_b))

# Noise status does survive relabelling, because -1 means the same in both.
print(((labels_a == -1) != (labels_b == -1)).sum(), "points changed noise status")
```

### Density on a grid

```python
ax.hexbin(df.lon, df.lat, gridsize=60, cmap="inferno", mincnt=1)
# gridsize is part of the claim. Put it in the caption.
```

### Embedding in Streamlit (Block 3)

```python
# app.py
import streamlit as st
from streamlit_folium import st_folium
import folium

state = st.sidebar.selectbox("State", sorted(df.state.unique()))
shown = df[df.state == state]

m = folium.Map(location=[shown.lat.mean(), shown.lon.mean()], zoom_start=6)
# One GeoJson layer, not one CircleMarker per point: same picture, a quarter
# of the page weight.
folium.GeoJson(points_geojson(shown)).add_to(m)
st_folium(m, width=700, height=450)

st.bar_chart(shown.groupby("city")["stalls"].sum().nlargest(10))
```

## 🏠 Homework — Weeks 9 and 10

One assignment covers both map modules. Build and deploy a multi-tab Streamlit
app on one point dataset, with at least two tabs. The requirements below are
what the app has to contain, not how to divide it between tabs.

The Supercharger locations in `week10/data/` are the default, and that folder
also holds state boundaries and an ACS table, so you can start without hunting
for anything.

The state is only the default unit, though. Aggregate to whatever boundary
interests you — counties, metro areas, census tracts, ZIP code areas — and work
somewhere other than the US if you would rather, with your own points. The
readings list above is where to look: `data.gov` for open data and boundary
files, Social Explorer for census and ACS tables with geographies to match,
TIGER/Line for US boundaries at any level.

Choosing your own region means finding three things rather than one — the
points, the boundaries, and a denominator for the rate — and all three have to
agree on how regions are identified. Same codes, same vintage. A FIPS column
stored as an integer has lost its leading zero and will match nothing, and a
2020 boundary file joined to a 2015 table drops every region that changed in
between. Both failures are silent, which is why requirement 2 asks for the
count of what did not match.

1. **A layered thematic map.** A choropleth carrying at least two layers of
   information — polygons encoding one measure, plus a second data layer over
   them: the points themselves, a heatmap, or graduated symbols. Basemap tiles
   do not count as a layer. folium, plotly or Altair, your choice.
2. **Both joins, each one shown.** A **spatial join** attaching the points to
   the regions that contain them, with a count of the points that matched
   nothing and an account of why they didn't. And an **attribute join** to an
   external dataset on a shared key, for normalization. `state_stats.csv` has
   population and a few other columns; join on `fips` or on the state name.
   Note that the boundary file already carries `land_sqmi`, so normalizing by
   area alone involves no join and does not satisfy this. Map the rate, and
   state your classification scheme and your projection.
3. **Captions.** Every map names what each layer encodes and the parameters
   behind it: projection, classification scheme and number of classes, heatmap
   radius or `eps` and `min_samples` if you used them, and anything you left
   out.
4. **One filter shared across tabs.** A sidebar control that moves more than
   one view.
5. **Deploy it** and submit the live URL plus the repo link to Blackboard.

**Bonus — up to 1 point.** Two routes; one is enough.

*A coordinated view.* Selecting in one chart updates another: click a state and
the distribution beside it refilters, or brush a scatter and the matching
regions highlight. Altair selection parameters,
`st.plotly_chart(on_select="rerun")`, and the click object `st_folium` hands
back all support this, so this route is open whichever library you picked.

*Clustering.* Run DBSCAN on the points and add the clusters to the map as a
further layer. Say which `eps` and `min_samples` you chose and why you chose
them — on this data that means deciding what counts as one metro area. Label
`-1` is noise rather than failure: report how many points it covers and what you
did with them, the same way you account for the points that matched no region.
The stronger version runs it twice with different `eps` and says what changed.
Cluster numbers are handed out in discovery order, so compare the groupings and
not the labels.

Other work past the required pattern counts too — the extensions below are a
good place to look.

**Rubric (10 pts)**

- Layered map: two data layers, both legible, both explained (3)
- Spatial join, with the unmatched points accounted for (2)
- External join and a correctly normalized rate (2)
- Multi-tab app, deployed, running without errors (2)
- Captions naming layers, projection, classification and parameters (1)
- Bonus: a coordinated view, DBSCAN clusters, or a comparable extension (+1)

The bonus offsets points lost elsewhere. The most this assignment can score
is 10.
